titre: The age of the Earth fit in a trace of lead
accroche: In 1956, a geochemist measures the age of the Earth at 4.55 billion years. In trying to refine it, he discovers something else entirely.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1956, the American geochemist Clair Patterson published an eight-page paper in *Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta*, titled “Age of meteorites and the earth.” The figure he calculates there, 4.55 billion years, give or take 70 million, remains the reference for the age of the Earth today.

## A lead clock

Patterson's method rests on the radioactive decay of uranium into lead, at a known and constant rate. Measuring the proportions of lead isotopes in a rock should therefore, in theory, make it possible to date its formation. The problem, on Earth, is that rocks have been recycled and reworked so many times by tectonics that they no longer record the age of the planet itself. Patterson gets around the obstacle by analyzing meteorites, in particular the Canyon Diablo meteorite, from Arizona, formed, like the Earth, from the same original dust cloud but geologically inert ever since. Their age is that of the solar system, and therefore, more or less, that of the Earth.

## An unexpected obstacle

To measure such minute traces of lead, Patterson must first make sure nothing contaminates his samples. He then discovers that lead is everywhere, in the air, in laboratory dust, even in his own reagents, at concentrations that make any reliable measurement impossible without a level of clean-room work unprecedented for the time. This hunt for contamination leads him to a discovery that goes far beyond the dating of meteorites: the lead in the ambient environment is not natural.

## The real impact

In 1962, Tsaihwa J. Chow and Patterson publish their first results. According to the National Academy of Sciences memoir, the amount of human-made lead released into the environment each year is then about eighty times the rate of deposit into ocean sediments, a calculation the authors call provisional because the data were too scarce or imprecise. Modern Greenland snow first appeared to contain more than a hundred times the lead of preindustrial snow, a figure later work with better-controlled blanks reduced to two. The source: leaded gasoline, blended into fuel since the early 1920s, mainly to raise its octane rating. Patterson then spends two decades documenting and publicly denouncing this contamination. Robert Kehoe, an Ethyl employee, calls him “more of a zealot than a scientist,” and Patterson is excluded from the 1971 National Research Council panel, whose makeup leaned too heavily, according to the memoir, toward industry scientists.

## What this shifts

The fight succeeds: the reduction of lead in gasoline begins around 1973, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announces in 1996 that, effective January 1, 1996, the Clean Air Act bans the sale of leaded gasoline for road vehicles. Off-road uses (aircraft, racing cars, farm equipment, marine engines) remain permitted. Patterson's most-cited result is therefore not the one we remember first, the date of the Earth's birth, but the one he brought to light while trying to refine it with enough rigor to notice that the ambient air should not have contained what it did.

repere.texte: In 1956, Clair Patterson calculates the age of the Earth at 4.55 billion years (± 70 million), from the lead in the Canyon Diablo meteorite, a figure still used today. While hunting down contamination in his samples, he discovers that the annual input of human-made lead is about 80 times the rate of deposit into ocean sediments, according to calculations that were then provisional.
repere.source: National Academy of Sciences, biographical memoir of Clair C. Patterson

carte.punch: He measured the age of the Earth, and discovered that the air shouldn't contain this.
carte.idee: In 1956, Clair Patterson calculates the age of the Earth at 4.55 billion years using the lead in a meteorite. In purifying his measurements, he discovers widespread contamination from leaded gasoline and spends two decades fighting it, until it leaves American roads.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: A fuller portrait of the man and of his clean-room measurement method.

quiz.question: Why did Clair Patterson use a meteorite rather than an Earth rock to date the Earth?
choix: Because Earth rocks have been recycled too much by tectonics to retain a record of the planet's age
Because no Earth rock contains a measurable amount of lead
Because meteorites are easier to date than rocks, whatever their origin
Because lead dating only works on extraterrestrial rocks
quiz.explication: Earth rocks have been melted, recycled, and reworked by plate tectonics: they therefore no longer record the age of the planet itself. Meteorites like Canyon Diablo formed at the same time as the Earth, from the same original cloud, but have remained geologically inert ever since.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why was gasoline leaded starting in the early 1920s?
choix: To lower the cost of refining fuel
To raise the fuel's octane rating
To extend the shelf life of the fuel
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Lead has been blended into fuel since the early 1920s, mainly to raise its octane rating. Patterson identified it as the source of the lead he kept finding everywhere, even in his own reagents.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the measurements published by Patterson and Chow in 1962 show?
choix: That the lead in the oceans came mostly from underwater volcanoes
That the annual human input of lead was about 80 times the ocean deposit
That Earth rocks had lost their lead through erosion
That laboratory air was cleaner than city air
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The annual input of human-made lead was about eighty times the rate of deposit into ocean sediments, according to calculations the authors called provisional.

quiz_supplementaire.question: From which panel was Patterson excluded in 1971?
choix: The Geological Society of America jury
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Patterson spent two decades denouncing this contamination. According to the National Academy of Sciences memoir, he was excluded from the 1971 National Research Council panel, which was too heavily weighted toward industry scientists.
